title: Hypercube Inc. (Mar 2015 TCC) Tax Court Canada Ruling
subject: Routine Programming Using Standard Techniques Does Not Qualify
summary: Hypercube Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 65, is a Tax Court of Canada decision denying a Canadian software company's $28,800 SR&ED wage claim for its taxation year ending April 30, 2012. For Canadian software claimants, the key takeaway is that routine programming resolved with standard techniques, unsupported by contemporaneous documentation and accurate time logs, does not qualify.
metaDescription: Explore the March 2015 Tax Court of Canada SR&ED decision for Hypercube Inc. and key takeaways for Canadian R&D tax claimants.

body.text: Section 1: Executive Summary and Case Background
Procedural Posture and Overview of the Dispute

In Hypercube Inc. v. Her Majesty The Queen, 2015 TCC 65 (2015 DTC 1089; Court File No. 2014-1254(IT)I), the Tax Court of Canada addressed the recurring tension between commercial software development and eligible Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) under the Canadian Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), as amended, hereinafter the "ITA"). Heard in Montréal, Quebec, on December 3, 2014, under the Court's Informal Procedure, and decided on March 17, 2015, by Associate Chief Justice Lucie Lamarre, the ruling stands as a foundational Canadian authority on two distinct pillars of SR&ED jurisprudence: the demarcation between technological uncertainty and routine software engineering, and the evidentiary weight accorded to time-tracking records and project documentation.

The appellant, Hypercube Inc., was a Canadian corporation operating in the computer software services sector with established expertise in programming websites. For its taxation year ending April 30, 2012, Hypercube filed an SR&ED claim on Form T661 seeking to qualify $28,800 in expenditures—consisting entirely of salary and wages paid to employees involved in developing a proprietary website inspection and verification software program—for SR&ED expenditure deductions and related investment tax credits (ITCs). Beginning conceptually in 2010 and moving into active internal discussions with employees at the start of 2012, the company's president, Mr. Villeneuve, spearheaded an initiative to construct a software program built around a web "crawler" designed to read, inspect, and analyze the source code of websites.
The Tax Authority's Challenge

Upon audit of the taxation year ending April 30, 2012, the Minister of National Revenue (the "Minister"), acting through the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), disallowed the entire $28,800 SR&ED expenditure claim and the corresponding ITCs. While the Minister permitted Hypercube to deduct the $28,800 as ordinary current business expenses in computing its net income under the ITA, the CRA refused to characterize the software development activities as SR&ED within the meaning of subsection 248(1) of the ITA.

The Minister's position rested on the technical assessment of CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) Mr. Roger Andria, who was called by the Crown as an expert witness at trial. Although Mr. Villeneuve objected to Mr. Andria's qualification as an expert witness—and Associate Chief Justice Lamarre found that he perhaps did not have the required expertise to give expert testimony in the specific field relevant to the case—the Court held that he could certainly testify as a CRA officer and give his reasons for determining that the project was not eligible for SR&ED credits under the applicable criteria. Mr. Andria testified that the appellant had developed a new product based on existing technology, that the program was developed from existing computer languages, and that the problems experienced during development were normal programming problems resolved using existing programming techniques, code correction being common practice in computer programming rather than a technological advancement. Furthermore, Mr. Andria stated that, in its hypotheses, the appellant did not define the technological uncertainties that were overcome and failed to explain how this represented a technological advancement in the field of computer science, while the Minister's position was that the project did not involve any technological advancement and instead involved resolving discrete problems within the constraints of the technologies used.
Governing Canadian Statutory and Jurisprudential Framework

The eligibility of R&D tax incentives in Canada is governed by a bifurcated statutory mechanism under the ITA. First, the technical work must satisfy the substantive definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the ITA. Second, once the technical work qualifies under subsection 248(1), the associated expenditures—such as directly attributable salaries and wages, materials consumed or transformed, and eligible contractor payments—are pooled for deduction under subsection 37(1) and generate Investment Tax Credits under subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the ITA, contingent upon prescribed filing requirements on Form T661.

Subsection 248(1) of the ITA defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" encompassing basic research, applied research, or experimental development undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Crucially, subsection 248(1) explicitly excludes commercial and routine technical activities under paragraphs (e) through (k), including market research or sales promotion (paragraph (e)), quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes (paragraph (f)), research in the social sciences or the humanities (paragraph (g)), prospecting, exploring or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum or natural gas (paragraph (h)), the commercial production of a new or improved material, device or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process (paragraph (i)), style changes (paragraph (j)), and routine data collection (paragraph (k)).

To operationalize subsection 248(1), Canadian courts apply the five cumulative criteria formulated by Judge Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. Canada, [1998] T.C.J. No. 340 (at paragraphs 14–16), which were subsequently cited with approval by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. Canada, [1998] F.C.J. No. 1590 (QL), 99 DTC 5087, at paragraph 10, and synthesized in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393. As reiterated by Associate Chief Justice Lamarre at paragraph 38 of Hypercube, a claimant must establish on a balance of probabilities that five distinct conditions were met. First, there must have been a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. Second, the person claiming to be doing SR&ED must have formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. Third, the procedure adopted must have accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses. Fourth, the process must have resulted in a technological advancement. Fifth, a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the results must have been kept as the work progressed.
The Court's Final Holding

Associate Chief Justice Lamarre dismissed Hypercube Inc.'s appeal in its entirety, affirming the Minister's assessment for the taxation year ending April 30, 2012. The Court held that Hypercube failed to demonstrate on a balance of probabilities that the development of its web-crawling and website verification software constituted SR&ED within the meaning of subsection 248(1) of the ITA. Specifically, Lamarre A.C.J. concluded that the taxpayer's activities did not transcend the limits of current technological standards, representing standard techniques generally accessible to competent professionals in the field rather than the product of a technological advancement. In addition, the Court observed at paragraph 48 that the appellant produced very little evidence documenting its project—only a program tree diagram that was not specifically explained in Court and a time log that recorded only the president's hours and did not appear to reflect reality—and that this evidence was not sufficient to support an SR&ED claim as prescribed by the ITA.
Section 2: Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures
Failure to Establish Technological Uncertainty Versus Routine Software Engineering

The primary substantive defect in Hypercube's claim was its inability to satisfy the threshold requirement of Northwest Hydraulic and C.W. Agencies: the existence of a genuine technological uncertainty that could not be resolved through publicly available knowledge, standard procedures, or routine engineering. Under Canadian SR&ED law and the administrative guidelines recognized by the Tax Court as a reliable interpretive aid—originally Information Circular IC 86-4R3 and subsequently the 2012 CRA Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (as confirmed in 6379249 Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 77 at paras. 57–58)—technological uncertainty arises only when whether a given result can be achieved, or how to achieve it, cannot be known or determined on the basis of generally available scientific or technological knowledge or experience. A claimant cannot merely assert that the exact code configuration was unknown prior to writing the software; the claimant must identify specifically what is lacking in the scientific or technological knowledge base that prevents a new or improved capability from being developed.

In Hypercube, the appellant was already experienced in website programming and sought to build a software utility that deployed a web crawler as the first step in reading and verifying website source code. Writing a web crawler to parse HTML or Document Object Model (DOM) structures and extract source code attributes is a well-documented, standard procedure in computer programming. During the hearing, the appellant's own testimony undermined its legal position: on cross-examination, Mr. Villeneuve acknowledged that crawlers are a commonly used tool in computer science (paragraph 16), and the difficulties he described—the program not working with certain domain names or certain Web browsers, a coding error that arose when the program was used more than 150 times a day, and Web sites automatically redirected to another URL—were resolved by changing or developing new code for the program (paragraphs 23–26). Relying on Judge Bowman's description in Northwest Hydraulic of routine engineering as techniques, procedures and data generally accessible to competent professionals in the field, Associate Chief Justice Lamarre found that the appellant's activities were generally accessible to competent professionals and that all the difficulties were resolved using recognized programming techniques, so that the work did not go beyond routine engineering or standard procedures (paragraphs 39 and 42–46).
The Holistic Project Fallacy and Component Aggregation

In its Notice of Appeal and oral submissions summarized at paragraph 35 of the judgment, Hypercube advanced a structural legal argument frequently attempted by software claimants: it alleged that its project consisted of a "series of related activities collectively required to achieve a technological advancement" and criticized the CRA auditor for dividing the software build into discrete subprojects and evaluating each as standard engineering practice.

The Tax Court did not expressly address this aggregation argument in its analysis; instead, it found that all the difficulties described by the appellant were resolved using recognized programming techniques and that the program's development did not go beyond the limits of current technological standards (paragraphs 44–46). While system-level architectural uncertainty can qualify as SR&ED when integrating disparate technologies creates unforeseen, non-linear system incompatibilities—such as the incompatibility in data-type mapping between .NET and Java platforms, not readily resolvable with existing accessible products, for which the Minister allowed SR&ED credits, as described in Highweb & Page Group Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 137—merely chaining together multiple routine software modules does not manufacture technological uncertainty. If each sub-component, such as URL fetching, source code parsing, rule validation, and reporting, relies on known algorithms and standard software design patterns, the aggregate software application remains routine engineering unless the integration itself encounters a fundamental technological barrier that standard software architecture cannot resolve.
Reliance on Trial and Error Rather Than Systematic Scientific Investigation

Under the second and third Northwest Hydraulic criteria, an eligible SR&ED project must be driven by the formulation of explicit scientific or technological hypotheses aimed at eliminating the technological uncertainty, executed through a systematic process of experimentation or analysis. In Hypercube, the evidence revealed that the appellant's employees developed the software through "trial and error".

Canadian tax jurisprudence draws a sharp doctrinal distinction between systematic experimental development and trial-and-error coding. Trial and error involves iteratively executing a series of tests or code changes in the hope of finding a working configuration without a governing causal model. In contrast, the scientific method mandated by subsection 248(1) requires a structured epistemic cycle in which the claimant defines the system-level parameters governing the technological failure, formulates a causal hypothesis explaining why the technological constraint occurs and predicting how a specific modification will resolve it, designs a controlled experiment or rigorous computational analysis to test that specific hypothesis, and conducts a systematic analysis to understand which requirement was not met and why each failed option fell short before formulating the subsequent hypothesis. Although the Court made no express finding on the trial-and-error methodology, Mr. Villeneuve described the work as retrieving one piece of information from a Web site's code, validating the attempt and then attempting to obtain the next piece of information (paragraph 20), and the Court found that each difficulty was resolved using recognized programming techniques that did not go beyond routine engineering or standard procedures (paragraphs 42 and 46).
Conflation of Commercial Product Novelty with Technological Advancement

At the hearing, Mr. Villeneuve—whose academic credentials consisted of a bachelor's degree in business administration, finance and marketing from Bishop's University and a Master of Business Administration (MBA) degree from the Université de Montréal, supplemented by several computer science courses and a certificate for technical computer training from Seneca College, rather than a degree in computer science or software engineering—testified that all work performed in developing the program constituted SR&ED because it improved the existing technology, which he described as various programming languages (paragraphs 18 and 35), while stating that the appellant had no short-term commercial goals (paragraph 28).

This argument conflates commercial or functional novelty—creating a new software product or adding new business features—with "technological advancement" under the fourth Northwest Hydraulic criterion. As the Tax Court has consistently held, including in Zeuter Development Corporation v. The Queen, 2006 TCC 597 at paragraphs 23 and 24, and reaffirmed in Hypercube (at paragraph 47) and Concept Danat Inc. v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 32 at paragraph 38, creating a new product or improving commercial functionality does not necessarily constitute a technological advancement. A technological advancement requires an advancement in general understanding or capability within the field of science or technology—even if that advance consists of the objective rejection after testing of a hitherto untested scientific hypothesis—rather than the routine application of existing technological knowledge to build a commercially useful website verification tool. Furthermore, the Court noted that the two people with a computer science background who worked on the program with Mr. Villeneuve—Jean-François Noël and Jean-Simon Lyonnais—did not appear in Court to give their scientific point of view regarding the project, leaving Mr. Villeneuve as the appellant's only witness (paragraphs 5 and 9).
Fatal Deficiencies in Contemporaneous Technical Documentation

The fifth Northwest Hydraulic criterion requires the taxpayer to maintain detailed records of the hypotheses tested and the experimental results as the work progresses. As the Tax Court emphasized in contemporaneous jurisprudence such as Highweb & Page Group Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 137 at paragraphs 20 and 22, a claimant is required to retain contemporaneous evidence demonstrating the chronological thought process pertaining to the work carried out. At paragraph 48 of Hypercube, Associate Chief Justice Lamarre noted that the appellant produced "very little evidence documenting its project". According to the Court, the only documents introduced in evidence to document the project—attached to the Notice of Appeal and filed as Exhibit I-1 at Tabs 5 and 8, alongside the appellant's T661 report at Tab 1 (paragraph 43)—were two artifacts: a "tree diagram" of the software program, which Mr. Villeneuve described as the work plan, and an Excel document showing the hours worked.

Although Mr. Villeneuve asserted that these two exhibits demonstrated all the hypotheses tested throughout the project, the Court found that this evidence was not sufficient to support an SR&ED claim as prescribed by the ITA. A static architectural tree diagram merely depicts the structural hierarchy or control flow of a software application at a single point in time; it does not record chronological experimental progression, baseline performance metrics, failed algorithmic branches, test logs, or analytical conclusions. Compounding this deficiency, the appellant failed to specifically explain the tree diagram in Court, leaving the trier of fact with an uncontextualized schematic that the Court did not accept as sufficient documentation of the project.
Defective Time-Tracking and Unsubstantiated Labour Expenditures

A frequently cited evidentiary observation in Hypercube is encapsulated in paragraph 48 regarding the substantiation of SR&ED salary and wage expenditures. Hypercube claimed $28,800 in wages paid to the employees who participated in developing the software program. However, upon judicial scrutiny of Exhibit I-1 (Tab 8), the Court identified two defects in the time-tracking records. First, although the expenditure claim encompassed wages paid to multiple employees who took part in developing the program, the time logs submitted into evidence recorded only the hours worked by Mr. Villeneuve, leaving no recorded hours for the other two people who worked on the program with him, Jean-François Noël and Jean-Simon Lyonnais (paragraphs 9, 10 and 27). Second, with respect to Mr. Villeneuve's own time log, Associate Chief Justice Lamarre explicitly found that "the time log does not appear to reflect reality". The Court did not elaborate on why the log did not appear to reflect reality, but it held that this evidence, together with the unexplained tree diagram, was not sufficient to support an SR&ED claim.

Consequently, Lamarre A.C.J. held at paragraph 48 that such evidence is insufficient to support an SR&ED claim as prescribed by the ITA. This specific holding has rippled through subsequent Canadian tax jurisprudence—most notably in Concept Danat Inc. v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 32 at paragraph 53, where Justice Lafleur, citing paragraph 48 of Hypercube, rejected a president's estimate that 10.2% of employees' time was spent on SR&ED and held that an accurate record of hours worked must be provided to support an SR&ED claim, adding that the description of the tasks performed by the various employees was not clear or sufficiently detailed to support the claim. Notably, Hypercube itself, quoting Zeuter Development at paragraph 28, acknowledged that supporting documentation is not absolutely necessary, although documentary evidence is the only reliable method of demonstrating that scientific research was undertaken in a systematic fashion.
Section 3: Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and jurisprudential requirement examined in Hypercube Inc. v. The Queen (2015 TCC 65) against the specific deficiencies in the taxpayer's claim and the evidentiary standard of proof enforced by the Tax Court of Canada.

headers: Taxpayer's Specific Failure in Hypercube Inc. (2015 TCC 65)
Tax Court of Canada Standard of Proof & Evidentiary Requirement

cells: 1. Technological Uncertainty (Existence of a systemic knowledge gap vs. routine engineering)
ITA s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 1); C.W. Agencies Inc. (2001 FCA 393)
Developed a web crawler to read and inspect website source code using standard programming techniques and commonly used tools. Argued that combining multiple subprojects holistically created SR&ED.

The claimant must prove on a balance of probabilities that the objective could not be achieved using publicly available knowledge, standard procedures, or routine analyses by competent programmers. The Court did not expressly rule on the holistic aggregation argument; it found that all difficulties were resolved using recognized programming techniques (paras. 44–46).
2. Formulation of Scientific Hypotheses (Targeted causal propositions)
ITA s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 2); RIS-Christie Ltd. (FCA)

Stated only a broad initial hypothesis that adopting a new way of performing Internet diagnostics would produce significant effects in terms of technological advancement (para. 13); the CRA's RTA testified that the hypotheses did not define the technological uncertainties overcome (para. 33). Relied on an unexplained program "tree diagram" as purported proof of hypotheses.

Hypotheses must be explicitly formulated prior to testing, identifying specific independent variables, system constraints, and testable causal predictions aimed directly at reducing or eliminating the technological uncertainty.
3. Discipline of the Scientific Method (Systematic investigation vs. trial and error)
ITA s. 248(1) ("systematic investigation or search... by means of experiment or analysis"); Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 3)

Mr. Villeneuve described the work as carried out methodically through "trial and error", retrieving and validating one piece of information at a time (para. 20); each difficulty was resolved by modifying code with recognized programming techniques (para. 46).

Work must follow an objective scientific methodology: hypothesis formulation, controlled testing, quantitative measurement, and root-cause analysis of why each failed iteration fell short before modifying the hypothesis.
4. Technological Advancement (Advancement in underlying technology vs. product utility)
ITA s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 4); Zeuter Development (2006 TCC 597)
Company president (an MBA) testified that all development work was SR&ED because it improved the existing technology, which he described as various programming languages (paras. 18 and 35).

The process must seek an advancement in the general understanding or capability of the underlying field of science or technology. Commercial novelty or building a new software product via standard techniques does not qualify.
5. Contemporaneous Technical Documentation (Artifact provenance and experimental logs)
Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 5); Hypercube Inc. (2015 TCC 65, para. 48)
Produced very little evidence documenting the project (para. 48). Entered only a static program tree diagram (Exhibit I-1, Tab 5) that was not specifically explained in Court (para. 48).

Contemporaneous records generated as the work progressed (e.g., dated git commit hashes, reverted experimental branches, benchmark test logs, failure analyses) must substantiate the chronological thought process.
6. Labour & Time-Tracking Substantiation (Allocation of eligible salaries and wages)
ITA ss. 37(1), 127(9), 248(1); Hypercube Inc. (2015 TCC 65, para. 48); Concept Danat (2019 TCC 32, para. 53)

Claimed $28,800 in wages for multiple employees, but the submitted time log (Exhibit I-1, Tab 8) recorded only Mr. Villeneuve's hours, and the Court stated that the time log does not appear to reflect reality (paras. 10 and 48).

An accurate, verifiable, and contemporaneous record of hours worked by every claimed employee, mapped directly to specific eligible SR&ED activities and tasks, is the reliable way to support an SR&ED wage claim; a time log covering only one employee that does not appear to reflect reality was held insufficient (para. 48).

body.text: Section 4: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To demonstrate how Canadian taxpayers and their advisors can operationalize the judicial lessons of Hypercube Inc. v. The Queen (2015 TCC 65), the following two industry case studies examine realistic projects vulnerable to the exact legal and evidentiary pitfalls identified by Associate Chief Justice Lamarre. Each case study provides a rigorous, step-by-step remedial blueprint across project governance, technical documentation, contract terms, and experimentation and labour tracking.
Case Study 1: Enterprise Automated Web-Scraping and DOM-Verification Engine (Software and SaaS Sector)
Project Scenario and Vulnerability to Hypercube Pitfalls

A Montréal-based Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC), "VeriCrawl Technologies Inc.," develops automated compliance-auditing software for financial institutions. In its current taxation year, VeriCrawl undertakes a project to build a high-concurrency crawler and Document Object Model (DOM) verification engine capable of inspecting single-page applications (SPAs) that dynamically render obfuscated JavaScript and WebAssembly state trees.

In its unguided state, VeriCrawl's project mirrors the exact fatal flaws that sank the taxpayer in Hypercube. First, the Vice President of Product, holding an MBA rather than a computer science degree, drafts the Form T661 narrative stating that the goal is to "develop a novel, automated website verification crawler that improves upon existing commercial compliance crawlers by auditing dynamic web pages faster". Second, the company aggregates $180,000 of developer salaries covering the user dashboard, database schema, standard headless browser integration, and the core state-inference engine, arguing that all sub-tasks are "collectively required" as a series of related activities to deliver the product. Third, developers adjust timeout parameters and DOM selectors by trial and error whenever headless browser instances crash, retaining only a high-level architectural UML tree diagram and a retrospective spreadsheet signed by the president estimating that four developers spent 60% of their annual hours on SR&ED.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint
Step 1: Project Governance and Boundary Segregation

To survive judicial scrutiny under Hypercube (paragraphs 35 and 40–47), VeriCrawl must immediately abandon the holistic product aggregation argument that the appellant unsuccessfully advanced in that case (paragraph 35) and institute formal project governance that segregates routine software development from eligible experimental development. Governance protocols must explicitly carve out the standard crawler transport layer, HTTP request scheduling, HTML and CSS parsing, database persistence, and user interface reporting dashboards as routine software engineering that does not constitute experimental development under paragraph 248(1)(c) of the ITA, with any quality control, routine testing, or routine data collection further excluded under paragraphs 248(1)(f) and (k). Simultaneously, the Technical Lead—a senior computer scientist rather than a business executive—must define the SR&ED project boundary strictly around the underlying technological uncertainty. Specifically, the governance charter must document why standard headless browser instrumentation (such as the Chromium DevTools Protocol) incurs exponential memory bloat and deterministic thread deadlock when attempting to reconstruct non-deterministic, asynchronous WebAssembly memory states across more than 500 concurrent worker nodes within a strict 150-millisecond execution window. By articulating that existing deterministic replay and symbolic execution algorithms in the public domain require full heap snapshots that exceed available input/output bandwidth by an order of magnitude, VeriCrawl establishes a genuine computer science knowledge gap rather than a routine coding task.
Step 2: Structuring the Process of Experimentation

To replace unguided trial-and-error coding with the scientific method mandated by Northwest Hydraulic Criteria 2 and 3, VeriCrawl must institute a mandatory four-stage experimental cycle for every development sprint. Prior to writing experimental code, the lead architect must formulate a testable causal hypothesis—for example, Hypothesis H-01, which posits that replacing full V8 heap snapshots with a custom differential shadow-stack interceptor hooked into WebAssembly linear memory growth events will bound memory overhead below 64 MB per worker while preserving 99.9% state-transition fidelity. Next, the team must establish quantitative baseline benchmarks measuring memory footprint in megabytes, CPU cycle latency in milliseconds, and state-graph completeness across a standardized corpus of 1,000 asynchronous test pages. When Hypothesis H-01 fails during testing due to race conditions in multi-threaded SharedArrayBuffer mutations, the engineering team is prohibited from simply trying random code configurations. Instead, they must execute and record a formal root-cause analysis proving why the lock-free shadow-stack failed under concurrent atomic operations, demonstrating that the rejection of Hypothesis H-01 generated new technological understanding that directly governs the formulation of Hypothesis H-02.
Step 3: Contemporaneous Technical Documentation Architecture

To avoid the evidentiary collapse seen in Hypercube (paragraph 48), where an unexplained static tree diagram was found insufficient by the Court, VeriCrawl must automate the capture of dated, immutable technical artifacts as the work progresses. The engineering team must enforce a strict Git version-control branching protocol in which all experimental work occurs within dedicated sred/exp-H01-* branches. Every commit message must reference the active hypothesis identifier, the independent variable modified, and the observed test metric, while failed experimental branches must never be deleted or squashed; they must be permanently archived with their commit hashes and timestamps intact to serve as contemporaneous proof of systematic investigation. Furthermore, Continuous Integration (CI) telemetry pipelines must automatically export dated performance logs comparing predicted versus actual memory and latency metrics for each experimental run, ensuring that every technical assertion in the Form T661 narrative traces directly to a verifiable artifact generated during the taxation year rather than a table created after the fact for the CRA audit.
Step 4: Granular Labour Tracking and Contractual Alignment

To address the deficiencies identified by Associate Chief Justice Lamarre at paragraphs 10 and 48, namely a time log that did not appear to reflect reality and that recorded the hours of only one of the people whose wages were claimed, VeriCrawl must deploy an integrated ticketing and time-logging system (such as Jira linked directly to Git commits). Every software developer and architect whose wages are claimed must log their hours daily against specific SR&ED experimental tickets (EXP-H01, EXP-H02) strictly segregated from routine commercial tickets (PROD-UI, PROD-CRAWLER), accompanied by a clear, detailed description of the exact experimental analysis or test performed and verified bi-weekly by the Technical Lead. Additionally, to protect ITC eligibility across contractual relationships, any Master Services Agreements (MSAs) and Statements of Work (SOWs) with Canadian software subcontractors assisting with low-level WebAssembly instrumentation must explicitly stipulate that the research is undertaken "on behalf of" VeriCrawl within the meaning of subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) of the ITA. The subcontractor agreements must vest all resulting intellectual property ab initio in VeriCrawl, place all financial and technological risk on VeriCrawl through time-and-materials billing rather than fixed-price commercial deliverables, and obligate the subcontractor to provide itemized timesheets matching VeriCrawl's SR&ED ticket taxonomy. Conversely, VeriCrawl's downstream SaaS customer agreements must be structured as standard commercial software subscriptions granting only a non-exclusive licence to use the commercial platform without funding or acquiring ownership of VeriCrawl's underlying R&D, thereby preventing customer revenues from being characterized as "contract payments" that would reduce qualified SR&ED expenditures under subsection 127(18) of the ITA.
Case Study 2: Industrial Laser-Guided Micro-Machining and Automated Optical Inspection System (Advanced Manufacturing Sector)
Project Scenario and Vulnerability to Hypercube Pitfalls

An Ontario-based precision manufacturing corporation, "OptiWeld Precision Ltd.," designs custom automated assembly lines. OptiWeld initiates a project to integrate a high-power industrial laser-ablation unit with an inline automated optical inspection (AOI) vision system to micro-texture and verify composite aerospace fasteners at high production line speeds.

OptiWeld's initial execution falls directly into the legal and evidentiary traps penalized in Hypercube and its direct progeny, Concept Danat Inc. v. The Queen (2019 TCC 32). First, shop-floor technicians adjust the existing settings on the commercial laser controller—such as air assist pressure, focal height, pulse frequency, and scan speed—across hundreds of permutations to stop the composite resin from charring. Because the technicians never go beyond the normal operating ranges of the commercial equipment or modify the laser optics and control firmware, their work constitutes routine machine calibration. Second, the technicians execute random combinations of settings on scrap fasteners by trial and error until a visually acceptable finish is achieved, without formulating physical or optical hypotheses. Third, at year-end, the company president estimates that the shop-floor supervisor and three technicians spent 25% of their time on the project, submitting only the president's personal logbook and a single, unexplained CAD layout diagram of the workcell.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint
Step 1: Project Governance and Redefining the Technological Baseline

To elevate the project from routine machine adjustment within normal operating ranges (as disqualified in Concept Danat at paragraphs 51–52, and analogous to the routine programming disqualified in Hypercube) to eligible SR&ED, OptiWeld's engineering governance committee must halt random parameter tuning and establish a formal Technological Baseline Assessment prior to claiming any SR&ED labour or materials. All hours spent testing the equipment manufacturer's recommended parameter matrix and standard operating ranges must be classified as non-eligible commercial setup and routine quality control under paragraph 248(1)(f) of the ITA. The governance committee must open the SR&ED project phase only after baseline testing proves that the commercial laser and vision hardware, operated at the outer bounds of their design specifications, cannot prevent subsurface thermal delamination while simultaneously capturing non-distorted optical interferometry data through the ablation plasma plume. The technological uncertainty is then rigorously defined around an opto-thermal coupling conflict: pulsed laser ablation at frequencies exceeding 50 kHz generates a transient refractive plasma plume that scatters the inline coaxial vision laser, rendering real-time closed-loop depth verification impossible using standard optical filters or vendor firmware.
Step 2: Implementing a Hypothesis-Driven Experimental Protocol

Rather than testing thousands of random combinations of laser speed and power by trial and error, OptiWeld's lead Metallurgical and Optical Engineer must institute a disciplined scientific protocol. Before any shop-floor trial is authorized, the engineer must formulate an explicit physical hypothesis—for example, Hypothesis H-01, which predicts that modulating the laser pulse train with a custom dual-wavelength picosecond burst envelope synchronized to a 405-nanometre narrow-band polarimetric strobe will suppress plasma plume refractive index gradients sufficiently to achieve sub-2-micron interferometric depth resolution at a line speed of 1.5 metres per second. Each experimental trial must isolate a single independent variable, such as inter-pulse delay in nanoseconds or polarization phase angle, while holding substrate composition and ambient gas flow constant. Following each trial, destructive cross-sectional scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) spectral analyses must be conducted to determine specifically which physical requirement was not met and why thermal micro-cracking or optical scattering persisted, using those quantitative analytical conclusions to modify the mathematical model for Hypothesis H-02.
Step 3: Contemporaneous Technical Evidence and Shop-Floor Trial Logs

To replace the unexplained schematic found insufficient in Hypercube (paragraph 48) with court-ready proof of systematic progression, OptiWeld must record every shop-floor test run in a dated, sequentially numbered SR&ED Experimental Logbook within its Manufacturing Execution System (MES) with immutable timestamps. Each experimental record must link the governing Hypothesis ID, the custom hardware or firmware modifications made to the laser pulse generator and optical path (accompanied by versioned optical schematics annotated to explain the exact physical change and its theoretical purpose), raw oscilloscope traces and interferometry SNR logs, and the engineer's post-test analytical conclusion. Concurrently, the MES must track the exact batch numbers and quantities of composite fasteners consumed or transformed during the experimental trials to substantiate eligible material expenditures under subsection 37(1) of the ITA, keeping experimental trial scrap strictly segregated from commercial production runs.
Step 4: Employee Time-Tracking Rigour and Commercial Contract Structuring

To ensure full compliance with paragraph 48 of Hypercube and paragraph 53 of Concept Danat, OptiWeld must eliminate management percentage estimates and single-person logs. Every engineer, programmer, and machinist participating in the SR&ED trials must clock in and out of dedicated SR&ED work orders on the shop-floor ERP terminal in real time as the work is performed. Each clock-out entry must include a mandatory technical task description linking the exact hours worked to the corresponding Experimental Run Sheet number—for example, recording 2.5 hours for machining a custom Brewster-angle polarizer mount and executing optical SNR calibration for Run #EXP-2026-04B—and restricting any claimed support labour strictly to tasks that are commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of the experimental trials under paragraph 248(1)(d) of the ITA. Finally, because OptiWeld is developing this laser micro-machining process while fulfilling a supply order for a Canadian aerospace Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM), its legal counsel must structure the commercial purchase agreement strictly as a contract for the sale of manufactured goods (aerospace fasteners) rather than a contract to perform R&D on behalf of the OEM. The supply contract must specify a fixed unit price per delivered fastener, explicitly state that the OEM acquires title solely to the physical fasteners with zero ownership or licensing rights to OptiWeld's custom laser-ablation process, optical firmware, or experimental data, and confirm that OptiWeld bears 100% of the financial risk if the experimental optical system fails to meet performance targets. This contractual architecture ensures that payments received from the aerospace OEM are treated as ordinary commercial sales revenue rather than "contract payments" under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, thereby preserving OptiWeld's unreduced entitlement to SR&ED Investment Tax Credits.
